title: A budget is just a plan, not a punishment
concept: A budget tells your money where to go instead of wondering where it went. It isn't about shame — it's clarity. Most anxiety around money comes from guessing, not from the numbers themselves.
takeaway: Naming your priorities makes spending feel intentional.

scenario.situation: Every month you swear you'll save more, but by day 20 your checking account is almost empty and you don't know why.

choices.text: Try harder next month without tracking anything
Track spending for one month, then assign every dollar a job
Only use credit cards so it doesn't feel real

feedback.A: Hope isn't a system. You need a simple map of in vs out.
feedback.B: Correct. Awareness first, then a plan. That's how budgets stick.
feedback.C: Credit doesn't erase spending — it delays and often adds interest.

scenario.lesson: You can't steer what you don't measure.

title: The 50/30/20 starting frame
concept: A common starter split: about 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings/debt payoff. It's a guideline, not gospel — adjust to your city, family, and goals.
takeaway: Separate needs from wants before debating small treats.

scenario.situation: After rent and groceries, you have $800 left. You want concerts, dining out, and to build an emergency fund.

choices.text: Spend freely — you'll save whatever is left
Decide a minimum savings amount first, then plan wants with what's left
Put 100% to savings and never enjoy life

feedback.A: Leftovers saving rarely works — lifestyle expands to fill the gap.
feedback.B: Correct. Pay your future self first, then enjoy the rest guilt-free.
feedback.C: All-or-nothing budgets usually snap. Sustainability beats perfection.

scenario.lesson: Automate or schedule savings so they aren't an afterthought.

title: Emergency funds: boring and powerful
concept: An emergency fund is cash you can access quickly when life happens — job loss, medical bills, a dead laptop. It keeps you from high-interest debt when the world gets loud.
takeaway: Start small, then grow to 3–6 months of essentials.

scenario.situation: You have $400 in savings and a $2,000 credit card limit. Your car needs $900 in repairs tomorrow.

choices.text: Put the repair on the card and worry about interest later
Use savings if you can, then rebuild the fund before extras
Skip the repair and hope for the best

feedback.A: Cards are a tool, but revolving balances turn shocks into long-term costs.
feedback.B: Correct. That's what the fund is for — then you refill it like a bill.
feedback.C: Avoiding the problem often makes it more expensive and dangerous.

scenario.lesson: Cash buffers turn emergencies into inconveniences.

title: Subscriptions that quietly drain you
concept: Small monthly charges feel harmless alone, but stacked they rival a rent increase. Auditing subscriptions is one of the fastest wins in personal finance.
takeaway: Cancel what you forgot you had. Keep what you truly use.

scenario.situation: You tally subscriptions and find $140/month in apps, boxes, and trials you barely touch.

choices.text: Ignore it — it's only a few dollars each
Cut or pause the low-value ones and redirect savings
Add more services to get 'better value'

feedback.A: $140/month is $1,680/year — real money that could fund goals.
feedback.B: Correct. Trim ruthlessly, keep joy on purpose.
feedback.C: More services rarely fix a leak — they multiply it.

scenario.lesson: Recurring charges deserve a quarterly review.

title: Sinking funds for predictable surprises
concept: A sinking fund is savings for expenses you know are coming — holidays, annual insurance, replacing a phone. You divide the cost across months so it never feels like a crisis.
takeaway: Predictable expenses shouldn't feel like emergencies.

scenario.situation: Your $1,200 annual insurance bill hits in November and wrecks your plan every year.

choices.text: Save $100/month into a labeled sinking fund
Skip insurance to free up cash

feedback.A: Annual bills are predictable — planning is kindness to your future self.
feedback.B: Correct. Smooth cash flow beats panic withdrawals.
feedback.C: Skipping coverage trades a small bill for huge tail risk.

scenario.lesson: Name the goal and automate the transfer.
